subject: chem
title: Organic Synthesis
subtitle: Multi-step synthesis, functional group interconversion and planning routes.
concept: Organic synthesis involves planning a series of reactions to convert a starting material to a target molecule, choosing appropriate reagents and conditions at each step.
Key transformations: alkene → halogenoalkane → alcohol → aldehyde/ketone → carboxylic acid → ester; nitrile → amine or carboxylic acid.
Purification and yield are important practical considerations.

notes.heading: Key Functional Group Interconversions
items: The most important transformations to know as a connected network: alkane → (UV/halogen) halogenoalkane; alkene → (HX) halogenoalkane; halogenoalkane → (NaOH aq) alcohol → (Cr₂O₇²⁻/H⁺, distil) aldehyde → (Cr₂O₇²⁻/H⁺, reflux) carboxylic acid; secondary alcohol → (Cr₂O₇²⁻/H⁺) ketone; halogenoalkane → (NaCN/ethanol) nitrile (+1C) → (LiAlH₄) amine or (HCl(aq) reflux) carboxylic acid.
For each step, always state: (i) reagent, (ii) conditions/solvent, (iii) type of reaction.

notes.heading: Multi-Step Synthesis and Retrosynthesis
items: Retrosynthetic analysis: work backwards from the target molecule. Identify the last bond formed or functional group introduced, then the step before that, and so on to a suitable starting material.
Key considerations: does the chain length need to change? (Use the nitrile route for +1C.) Does stereochemistry matter? Is the target chiral — can HCN addition give the needed enantiomer?
Atom economy and percentage yield apply to each step — multi-step syntheses accumulate losses.

notes.heading: Purification and Purity
items: Purification methods: distillation (for liquids with different boiling points), recrystallisation (for solids — dissolve in minimum hot solvent, cool slowly to get pure crystals), column chromatography.
Test for purity: sharp melting point at the expected value (impurities lower and broaden the melting point range). GC retention time or TLC Rf compared with a pure reference sample.

definitions.body: Working backwards from the target molecule to identify synthetic routes and starting materials.
(Actual moles of product / theoretical moles of product) × 100%.

workedExamples.q: Outline the conversion of bromoethane to ethylamine in two steps via a nitrile.

steps.text: CH₃CH₂Br + NaCN (ethanol) → CH₃CH₂CN + NaBr (nucleophilic substitution → propanenitrile).
CH₃CH₂CN + 4[H] (LiAlH₄, then H₂O) → CH₃CH₂CH₂NH₂ (propylamine) — reduction of nitrile.
This sequence extends the chain by one carbon AND introduces –NH₂.

mistakes: Losing track of carbon chain length — always count C atoms in reactant and product.
Using the wrong oxidation state conditions — distil for aldehyde, reflux for carboxylic acid.
Forgetting that NaCN increases the chain length by 1 carbon.
tips: Learn the 'ladder' of oxidation states: alkane → (UV/X₂) halogenoalkane → (NaOH aq) alcohol → (Cr₂O₇²⁻) aldehyde → carboxylic acid.
For each step: state (i) reagent, (ii) conditions/solvent, (iii) type of reaction.
A nitrile route: halogenoalkane → nitrile (+1C) → amine (LiAlH₄) OR carboxylic acid (HCl reflux or NaOH then acid).

flashcards.q: What reagent converts an aldehyde to a primary alcohol?
flashcards.a: NaBH₄ (sodium borohydride) in aqueous/ethanol — nucleophilic addition/reduction.

flashcards.q: How do you increase the carbon chain length by one carbon from a halogenoalkane?
flashcards.a: React with NaCN (in ethanol) → nitrile (RCN); the nitrile has one more carbon than the halogenoalkane.
Working backwards from the target molecule to identify the starting material and reagents for each step.

flashcards.q: What conditions convert a nitrile to a carboxylic acid?
flashcards.a: Reflux with HCl(aq) (or NaOH(aq), then acidify) → RCOOH + NH₄⁺ (or NH₃).

flashcards.q: How do you test purity of an organic solid?
flashcards.a: Measure the melting point: pure substance melts sharply at the expected temperature; impurities lower and broaden the melting point range.

flashcards.q: What is the reagent for converting a carboxylic acid to an ester without a catalyst?
flashcards.a: Use an acyl chloride + alcohol (no catalyst needed — faster than esterification with H₂SO₄).

questions.q: What reagents convert CH₃CH₂Br to CH₃CH₂OH?
questions.exp: Warm aqueous NaOH: nucleophilic substitution replacing Br⁻ with OH⁻ → alcohol.

questions.q: How would you convert ethanol to ethanoic acid in one step?
questions.exp: Refluxing ethanol with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ oxidises first to ethanal, then further to ethanoic acid.

questions.q: A student wants to make butanenitrile from 1-bromopropane. What reagent is needed?
questions.exp: NaCN in ethanol: 1-bromopropane (3C) + CN⁻ → butanenitrile (4C) + Br⁻.

questions.q: Which sequence converts propan-1-ol to propan-1-amine?
opts: Oxidise to acid, then react with PCl₅, then NH₃
questions.exp: propan-1-ol → propanoic acid (reflux, Cr₂O₇²⁻) → propanoyl chloride (PCl₅) → propanamide (NH₃) → propylamine (LiAlH₄).

questions.q: What is % yield if 3.6 g of product is obtained when 6.0 g is theoretically possible?
You want to increase the carbon chain length by 1 carbon from a halogenoalkane. Which reagent is used?
questions.exp: RX + KCN → RCN + KX (nucleophilic substitution). The CN⁻ ion acts as a nucleophile, adding one carbon via a nitrile group. The nitrile can then be hydrolysed (→ carboxylic acid) or reduced (→ amine).

questions.q: What is the purpose of 'retrosynthetic analysis'?
opts: To work backwards from the target molecule to identify suitable starting materials
questions.exp: Retrosynthesis (disconnection approach) works backwards: identify the target, disconnect a bond to reveal simpler precursors, repeat until commercially available starting materials are reached. This maps out the synthetic route efficiently.

questions.q: Which sequence converts ethanol to ethanoic acid?
opts: Oxidation with K₂Cr₂O₇/H₂SO₄, distill → aldehyde, then oxidise under reflux → acid
questions.exp: Ethanol (primary alcohol) → ethanal (aldehyde) by oxidation with K₂Cr₂O₇/H₂SO₄ with distillation. Ethanal → ethanoic acid by further oxidation under reflux. Both steps use acidified dichromate.

questions.q: How would you convert a carboxylic acid to an amine in one overall transformation?
opts: React with PCl₅ then with excess NH₃
React with SOCl₂ to make acid chloride, then with NH₃ to make amide, then reduce amide with LiAlH₄
Direct reaction with NH₃ in water
questions.exp: RCOOH → RCOCl (SOCl₂) → RCONH₂ (NH₃) → RCH₂NH₂ (LiAlH₄). This 3-step route keeps the same carbon count. Alternatively, RCOOH → RCN (+1C) → RCH₂NH₂ if chain extension is acceptable.

questions.q: A compound melts sharply at the expected melting point and gives a single spot by TLC. This indicates:
opts: The compound is a mixture of enantiomers
questions.exp: A sharp melting point at the expected value (small range, <1–2 °C) and a single TLC spot (single Rf) both indicate a pure compound. Impurities lower and broaden the melting point and give additional TLC spots.

questions.q: Starting from bromobenzene, which sequence gives phenylamine?
questions.exp: Bromobenzene → nitrobenzene via electrophilic nitration (HNO₃/H₂SO₄)? No — bromobenzene can't be directly converted this way. The direct route to phenylamine from benzene is: benzene → nitrobenzene (HNO₃/H₂SO₄) → phenylamine (Sn/HCl then NaOH).

questions.q: In a multi-step synthesis, overall yield = product of individual step yields. If 3 steps each give 80% yield, what is the overall yield?
questions.exp: Overall yield = 0.80 × 0.80 × 0.80 = 0.512 = 51.2%. This shows why minimising the number of steps is important in industrial synthesis — each step's imperfect yield multiplies the losses.

questions.q: What functional group is introduced when a halogenoalkane reacts with hot ethanolic KOH?
questions.exp: Hot ethanolic KOH promotes elimination: OH⁻ acts as a base, abstracting an H adjacent to the C–X; HX is eliminated to form an alkene. Conditions: concentrated KOH, ethanol solvent, heat.

questions.q: Which reagent converts an alcohol into a halogenoalkane with inversion of configuration?
questions.exp: SOCl₂ converts –OH to –Cl with retention of carbon skeleton and, in SN2 mechanism, inversion at the chiral centre. It's cleaner than HCl/HBr because the by-products (SO₂ and HCl) are gases that leave the reaction mixture.

questions.q: To make a racemic mixture from a ketone by nucleophilic addition of HCN, the product is:
questions.exp: HCN adds to the C=O from both faces equally (the sp² carbonyl is planar). Attack from opposite faces gives opposite configurations at the new chiral centre → equal amounts of (R) and (S) enantiomers = racemic mixture.

questions.q: To extend a carbon chain by one carbon from a halogenoalkane, which reagent is used?
questions.exp: RX + KCN/ethanol → RCN + KX. The CN⁻ nucleophile adds one carbon, giving a nitrile (and eventually a carboxylic acid or amine).

questions.q: Which conditions convert a primary alcohol to a carboxylic acid?
questions.exp: Primary alcohol + acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ under reflux (prevents aldehyde from escaping) → carboxylic acid. Distillation gives the aldehyde only.

questions.q: A secondary alcohol is oxidised by acidified K₂Cr₂O₇. The product is:
questions.exp: Secondary alcohols are oxidised to ketones. Ketones cannot be oxidised further under normal conditions.

questions.q: Retrosynthesis of ethyl ethanoate (CH₃COOC₂H₅) — which two starting materials are needed?
questions.exp: Ester name: ethyl (from ethanol) ethanoate (from ethanoic acid). Esterification: CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O.

questions.q: To convert a nitrile (RCN) to a carboxylic acid (RCOOH), you would:
questions.exp: RCN + H₂O (acid/base catalyst, reflux) → RCOOH. The nitrile is hydrolysed. LiAlH₄ gives the amine instead.

questions.q: Which reagent converts an ester to a carboxylic acid irreversibly?
questions.exp: Base hydrolysis (saponification): ester + NaOH → sodium carboxylate + alcohol. Irreversible because the carboxylate cannot re-esterify.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a multi-step synthesis rather than a direct one-step conversion?
opts: To bypass functional groups that cannot be interconverted directly
questions.exp: Many functional group interconversions are not possible in one step. Multi-step routes allow access to target molecules via a series of achievable transformations.

questions.q: A compound has an –OH group and a –COOH group on the same molecule. It can form:
questions.exp: A hydroxy acid (e.g. lactic acid) can polymerise by repeated esterification between –OH and –COOH groups of different molecules, forming a polyester.

questions.q: Percentage yield = 60% means:
opts: You obtained 60% of the theoretical maximum product
questions.exp: % yield = (actual moles of product / theoretical moles) × 100. 60% means 60% of the maximum possible product was actually isolated.

questions.q: To confirm the identity of a purified solid product, you would measure its:
opts: Melting point and compare with literature
questions.exp: A pure solid has a sharp melting point at the known literature value. Impurities lower and broaden the melting point range.

recall: List four functional group interconversions you can perform starting from a halogenoalkane.
Describe how to extend a carbon chain by one using the nitrile route.
Calculate % yield from actual and theoretical masses.
Describe how to test the purity of an organic product.
